card: Paper card. Question: How does increasing chemical disorder and compositional complexity in single-phase concentrated solid solution alloys (SP-CSAs) affect energy dissipation pathways and subsequent defect evolution under ion irradiation?. System: Single-phase fcc concentrated solid solution alloys: elemental Nickel (Ni), binary NiCo, binary NiFe, and quaternary NiCoFeCr (all equiatomic), plus non-equiatomic Ni0.65Fe0.35 and Ni0.40Fe0.60.. Processing: High-purity elemental metals arc melted and drop cast into copper moulds; single crystals directionally solidified in an optical floating zone furnace under Ar atmosphere; polished to damage-free surfaces for ion channelling.. Test conditions: Room temperature irradiation using 3 MeV Au2+ ions (fluence 1-2 × 10^13 cm^-2) and 1.5 MeV Ni+ ions (fluence 6 × 10^13 to 2 × 10^14 cm^-2); electrical resistivity measured between 5 K and 300 K; thermal conductivity measured at room temperature; in situ ion channelling and high-resolution TEM characterization.. Findings: Electrical resistivity at 5 K increases from ~0.1 μΩ cm for Ni to 77.1 μΩ cm for NiCoFeCr, indicating a substantial reduction in electron mean free path.; Total thermal conductivity at 300 K decreases from 88 W m−1 K−1 for Ni to 12.8 W m−1 K−1 for NiCoFeCr.; Backscattering yield (damage indicator) for NiFe is approximately half that of pure Ni after 3 MeV Au irradiation.; Stable defect production in NiFe is ~2 times lower than in pure Ni according to molecular dynamics cascade simulations.; Quaternary NiCoFeCr shows ~5 times less accumulated damage than pure Ni under Ni ion irradiation.; Increasing Fe concentration from 35% to 60% in Ni-Fe alloys enhances irradiation resistance.; Stacking fault tetrahedra (SFT) sizes are smaller in alloys (4.3-4.4 nm) compared to pure Ni (7.0 nm) due to slower defect migration.. Mechanism: Chemical disorder in SP-CSAs causes significant smearing of the electronic band structure (Bloch spectral function), reducing the electron mean free path and drastically lowering electronic thermal conductivity. This leads to less efficient heat dissipation, prolonging the lifetime of thermal spikes generated by ion collisions. The extended thermal spike duration and localized energy deposition alter defect energetics, increasing migration barriers and formation energies, which suppresses the clustering of point defects into larger, deleterious structures.. Limitations: The study focuses on simple fcc lattice structures and early-stage defect dynamics; the authors note that the results should not be interpreted as HEAs being intrinsically more radiation resistant in all cases, but rather that complexity is a tunable parameter for modifying transport properties.. Future work: The authors propose further exploration to understand how chemistry and composition can alter energy dissipation mechanisms to drive self-recovery from damage states, aiming to design radiation-resistant alloys by controlling coupling strengths and defect energetics at the atomic and electronic levels.. Quote: "much slower energy dissipation results in less deleterious defects and consequent slower damage accumulation under ion irradiation."

W2938633511.title: High entropy alloys as a bold step forward in alloy development

card: Paper card. Question: What is the origin of the superior strength and plasticity in the CrCoNi alloy compared to the CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy, and how do magnetic properties influence the phase stability between fcc and hcp structures?. System: CrCoNi (ternary), CrMnFeCoNi (quinary), FeCoNi, MnCoNi, MnFeNi (equiatomic ternary derivatives). Processing: Alloys prepared as single-phase fcc solid solutions; samples deformed to approximately 55% true strain; DFT calculations using VASP with GGA-PBE, quasi-harmonic approximation for vibrational entropy, and special quasi-random structures (SQS); atomistic simulations using classical potentials on fcc Co as a surrogate.. Test conditions: Cryogenic to room temperature regimes relevant to experiments; shear deformations inducing stacking faults and twin interfaces; magnetic and non-magnetic DFT calculations; atomic resolution STEM in HAADF mode along 110 and 101 zone axes.. Findings: CrCoNi exhibits a distinctly lower-energy hcp phase compared to fcc at low temperatures, driven by vibrational entropy, whereas CrMnFeCoNi shows negligible energy difference due to magnetic frustration.; In CrCoNi, the hcp phase is favored over fcc even when magnetic effects are turned off, while in Mn-containing alloys (MnCoNi, MnFeNi), magnetism reduces the energy difference between phases to nearly zero.; Mn atoms exhibit magnetic frustration with moments fluctuating between approximately 3 and -3 μB regardless of environment, unlike Cr moments which show a narrower distribution and stronger dependence on local chemistry.; The average stacking fault energy in CrCoNi is negative, indicating a driving force for fcc-to-hcp transformation, whereas in CrMnFeCoNi, energy overlaps between stable and unstable structures prevent a clear driving force.; Hcp laths in CrCoNi form localized to stacking faults and twin interfaces via the glide of 1/6<112> Shockley partial dislocations, rather than as a bulk transformation.; Dislocation interactions with twin boundaries in CrCoNi lead to the nucleation of 3-layer hcp structures, which act as barriers to slip while redirecting shear to prevent stress concentration.; The hcp phase in CrCoNi can heal back to fcc upon removal of stress or interaction with intersecting slip systems, allowing for recovery without loss of plasticity.. Mechanism: The authors propose that the superior mechanical properties of CrCoNi arise from a magnetically-driven fcc-to-hcp phase transformation triggered by dislocation slip. In CrCoNi, the hcp phase is intrinsically lower in energy (ground state) at low temperatures, and the absence of magnetic frustration allows this transformation to proceed readily at stacking faults and twin boundaries. This creates nanostructured hcp laths that strengthen the material by blocking dislocations while simultaneously redirecting shear to avoid crack initiation. In contrast, the addition of Mn in CrMnFeCoNi introduces magnetic frustration, which eliminates the energy difference between fcc and hcp phases, suppressing the transformation and resulting in inferior mechanical performance.. Limitations: Free energy calculations for the quinary CrMnFeCoNi alloy pose significant practical challenges and yielded non-conclusive estimates; the study uses fcc Co as a surrogate system for atomistic simulations of dislocation interactions in CrCoNi due to the lack of reliable interatomic potentials for the Ni-Co-Cr system.. Future work: The authors suggest that new alloying combinations can be predicted based on favorable magnetic properties to design single-phase alloys with metastable structures, emphasizing that high-entropy alloys with more constituent elements are not necessarily superior to their derivatives.. Quote: "This highlights the unique combination of chemistry and magnetic properties in CrCoNi, leading to a fcc-hcp phase transformation that occurs only in this alloy."

W2913404911.title: Uncovering electron scattering mechanisms in NiFeCoCrMn derived concentrated solid solution and high entropy alloys

card: Paper card. Question: How do the type and number of elements in Ni-based single-phase equiatomic alloys affect their electrical, thermal, and magnetic properties, particularly regarding the role of chemical and magnetic disorder?. System: Eight Ni-based FCC equiatomic alloys: elemental Ni, NiCo, NiFe, NiCoFe, NiCoCr, NiCoFeCr, NiCoFeCrMn, and NiCoFeCrPd. Processing: Arc-melting of pure elemental metals (>99.9% pure) followed by five flips and re-melts, drop-casting into a copper mold, and conversion to single crystals or polycrystalline rods via optical floating zone furnace; samples cut to ~1 × 1 × 10 mm3 and electrolytically polished. Test conditions: Electrical resistivity and thermal conductivity measured from 4 to 300 K; magnetization measured in magnetic fields up to 4 T from 4 to 300 K. Findings: Resistivities of alloys containing Cr (e.g., NiCoCr, NiCoFeCr) are about one order of magnitude larger than those without Cr (e.g., NiCoFe, NiFe).; The residual resistivity does not strongly correlate with the number of elements; the addition of Cr rapidly increases resistivity while Co has limited effects.; Thermal conductivities of the alloys are largely lower than pure metals primarily because high electrical resistivity suppresses the electronic thermal conductivity.; In concentrated alloys, lattice thermal conductivity (κg) dominates at low temperatures and is comparable to electronic thermal conductivity (κe) at room temperature.; The NiCoFeCrMn alloy exhibits a resistivity minimum at ~25 K, suggesting Kondo-like behavior or a spin glass transition.; NiCoCr is paramagnetic above 4 K, while NiCoFeCr has a Curie temperature (Tc) of ~120 K.; The addition of Cr significantly reduces magnetization due to magnetic cancellation, as Cr moments are anti-parallel to Ni, Co, and Fe moments.. Mechanism: High residual resistivity in alloys containing Cr and Mn is strongly attributed to magnetic disorder, where the presence of antiferromagnetically coupled elements (Cr, Mn) alongside ferromagnetically coupled elements (Ni, Co, Fe) creates strong scattering potentials for both spin-up and spin-down electrons, shortening the electron mean-free-path.. Limitations: The KKR-CPA calculations neglect displacement fluctuations, which may contribute to residual resistivity, particularly in alloys with large atomic size mismatches like NiCoFeCrPd.. Future work: Further studies are needed to investigate the origin of the finite positive TCR at low temperatures in NiCoCr, and additional experiments (ac susceptibility, heat capacity, neutron scattering) are required to conclusively determine the nature of the transition near 25 K in NiCoFeCrMn.. Quote: "The scattering of electrons is significantly increased due to the chemical (especially magnetic) disorder."

card: Paper card. Question: How do the phonon dynamics of the high-entropy alloy FeCoCrMnNi compare to those of glasses and complex metallic alloys (CMAs), and does it represent a unique class of materials?. System: Fe20Co20Cr20Mn20Ni20 (FeCoCrMnNi), a 5-element equiatomic FCC random solid solution. Processing: Polycrystalline samples produced by alloying high-purity elements in an inductively coupled high-frequency levitation furnace, slip-cast into a water-cooled copper mold, and annealed at 1200 °C for 48 h; single crystals grown via the Bridgman technique at 1340 °C with a solidification velocity of 50 mm/h under 200 mbar argon. Test conditions: Measurements performed at temperatures of 3, 15, 100, 200, and 300 K using inelastic neutron scattering (INS) and inelastic X-ray scattering (IXS); energy ranges up to 30 meV and wavevectors covering the Brillouin zone. Findings: Acoustic phonons propagate as well-defined modes throughout the entire Brillouin zone up to energies of 20–30 meV.; Phonon linewidths (ΓFWHM) are significantly broader than in simple monatomic elements but similar to binary alloys of the same constituents.; The observed phonon broadening is primarily attributed to force-constant fluctuations estimated at ~20%, while mass fluctuations contribute negligibly (<0.2 meV).; Phonon attenuation exhibits anisotropy, with longitudinal modes showing multiple regimes and transverse modes showing a smoother monotonic increase.; A strong scattering regime following ΓFWHM ∝ (ℏω)4.5±1 is observed up to ~18 meV in the [ζ00] direction, transitioning to (ℏω)1.7±0.2 above this energy.; The Ioffe-Regel limit (where mean free path equals wavelength) occurs only at energies above ~30 meV, much higher than in typical glasses.; The Generalized Vibrational Density of States (GVDOS) shows a linear dependence up to ~12 meV at low temperatures due to magnetic scattering, reverting to Debye-like (ℏω)2 behavior at room temperature.. Mechanism: The authors argue that the strong phonon attenuation is driven by force-constant fluctuations resulting from the random atomic environment, which are enhanced by the specific chemical disorder of the alloy. This mechanism is distinct from glasses where topological disorder is also present, and from CMAs where the acoustic phase space is reduced by optic modes. The authors note that the force-constant fluctuations per atomic pair (20–50%) are comparable to those in binary alloys, suggesting that increasing the number of elements from 2 to 5 does not necessarily increase phonon attenuation as predicted by some theories.. Limitations: The study notes that the strong incoherent neutron scattering entangled with the acoustic phonon in neutron data made the fitting procedure challenging for extracting linewidths, necessitating reliance on IXS data. Additionally, the theoretical models used could not reliably reproduce the low-q part of the spectrum due to the small supercell size used in simulations.. Future work: The authors propose that larger force-constant fluctuations should be sought by choosing elements with more different characteristics to effectively impact phonon engineering, noting that current HCP and BCC HEAs introduce stronger mass and atomic size disorder that prevents force-constant disorder from dominating.. Quote: "HEAs present unique phonon dynamics at the frontier between fully disordered and ordered materials, characterized by long-propagating acoustic phonons in the whole Brillouin zone."

card: Paper card. Question: How does increasing the atomic size difference (δ) affect the microstructure stability, grain growth activation energy, and mechanical properties of single FCC phase high-entropy alloys?. System: CoCrFeMnNi (δ=1.18%), Al0.2CoCrFeMnNi (δ=2.77%), and Al0.3CoCrCu0.3FeNi (δ=3.65%). Processing: Arc melting at 500 A in 0.01 Torr vacuum, homogenization at 1100 °C for 6 h, water quenching or furnace cooling, cold rolling with 70% thickness reduction, and annealing between 900 °C and 1100 °C for various times followed by water quenching. Test conditions: Tensile testing at ambient temperature with a strain rate of 10⁻³ s⁻¹; grain growth analysis via annealing at 900–1100 °C for various durations. Findings: The atomic size difference increased from 1.18% in CoCrFeMnNi to 2.77% in Al0.2CoCrFeMnNi and 3.65% in Al0.3CoCrCu0.3FeNi.; The activation energy of grain growth for Al0.2CoCrFeMnNi was calculated to be 434.4 kJ/mol.; The activation energy of grain growth for Al0.3CoCrCu0.3FeNi was the highest among the three alloys at 761.3 kJ/mol.; Al0.3CoCrCu0.3FeNi exhibited a yield strength of 500 MPa and ultimate tensile strength of 717 MPa after annealing at 900 °C for 5 h.; All three alloys maintained a single FCC phase structure after homogenization and cooling, showing good workability with 70% cold rolling reduction without cracks.; The grain size of Al0.3CoCrCu0.3FeNi after annealing at 1000 °C for 120 min was not explicitly stated as a single value in the text, but the activation energy calculation was based on grain sizes measured at different temperatures and times.. Mechanism: The authors argue that a large atomic size difference causes high lattice distortion, which increases the energy level of the grain compared to an undistorted state. This creates a higher driving force requirement for recrystallization, leading to higher activation energy for grain growth. Additionally, solute atoms (particularly Al) act as obstacles that pin dislocations in stable lattice sites, increasing strength through solid solution hardening and the pinning effect.. Limitations: The text states that 'the lattice distortion effect on properties of HEAs is yet an open question still await to be solved'.. Quote: "The activation energy of grain growth is 761.3 kJ/mol."

card: Paper card. Question: How does the presence of local chemical order (LCO) influence the formation, evolution, and recombination of irradiation-induced point defects and defect clusters in equiatomic CrCoNi medium-entropy alloys compared to a random solid solution?. System: Equiatomic CrCoNi medium-entropy alloy (MEA) in two states: water-quenched (approximated as a random solid solution, RSS) and aged at 1,000 °C for 120 h (LCO CrCoNi); pure Ni used as a benchmark.. Processing: Raw ingot homogenized at 1,200 °C for 48 h; split into two treatments: (1) water quenched to room temperature to form RSS; (2) aged at 1,000 °C for 120 h followed by slow furnace cooling to induce LCO. Ion irradiation performed in situ at 300 K using 50 keV He+ ions. Atomistic simulations prepared RSS by random distribution and LCO via MD/MC at 1,300 K with variance-constrained semigrand canonical ensemble.. Test conditions: In situ TEM irradiation at 300 K with 50 keV He+ ions up to 1.0 dpa; MD simulations of primary damage with PKA energies of 5, 10, 20, and 40 keV; diffusion simulations at various temperatures (including 1,200 K) to measure vacancy and interstitial mobility.. Findings: The areal fraction of LCO regions is approximately 3% in water-quenched RSS CrCoNi versus ~30% in the 1,000 °C-aged LCO CrCoNi.; At a low irradiation dose of 0.16 dpa, the LCO sample is nearly defect-free while the RSS sample already contains visible defect clusters.; The number density of defect clusters in the LCO sample is significantly smaller than in the RSS sample across the entire dose range of 0.16 to 1.0 dpa.; The average activation energy for interstitial diffusion increases from 0.22 eV in RSS to 0.34 eV in LCO, while for vacancies it increases from 0.69 eV to 0.76 eV.; The difference in activation energy between interstitial and vacancy diffusion narrows from 0.47 eV in RSS to 0.42 eV in LCO, reducing the mobility ratio.; The correlation factor for interstitial diffusion decreases by 29% (from 0.232 to 0.165) in LCO compared to RSS, indicating stronger localization of interstitial motion.; Large-sized defect clusters (Ncluster > 30) are suppressed in LCO CrCoNi, with the number of point defects in large clusters being ~35% lower than in RSS.; The recombination rate of Frenkel pairs at the end of the thermal spike is nearly identical for RSS and LCO (~99.6%), but the LCO sample retains fewer surviving FPs due to enhanced recombination during the cooling phase.. Mechanism: The authors argue that LCO enhances irradiation resistance through a two-pronged kinetic effect: (1) it increases migration energy barriers, slowing down the diffusion of both vacancies and interstitials (localizing their motion); and (2) it narrows the mobility ratio between interstitials and vacancies (by affecting interstitials more strongly), which increases the probability of their recombination and annihilation during the cooling phase of the collision cascade, thereby reducing the number of surviving defects and large clusters.. Limitations: The study notes that small-sized defect clusters (Ncluster < 8) are not detectable by in-situ TEM due to resolution limits and are susceptible to dissolution, so the comparison between experiment and simulation focuses on large-sized clusters. The extent of LCO investigated is limited to chemical short-range order (CSRO) developed via the specific aging treatment.. Future work: The authors propose that tailoring composition and heat treatment to extend LCO beyond CSRO into medium-range or long-range order, or adding interstitial alloying elements (such as C, N) with chemical affinity for specific constituents, could further boost irradiation tolerance.. Quote: "increased local chemical order (e.g., via thermal aging) significantly enhances their resistance to irradiation damage by narrowing the mobility ratio of irradiation-induced interstitials and vacancies that can facilitate their recombination."

card: Paper card. Question: What distinguishes multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs) from traditional solid solutions, and how does local chemical order (LCO) influence dislocation behavior and mechanical strength?. System: FCC NiCoCr medium-entropy alloy (equiatomic composition). Processing: Hybrid molecular dynamics (MD) and Monte Carlo (MC) simulations with annealing temperatures (Ta) ranging from 650 K to 1650 K; empirical embedded-atom method (EAM) potential developed without spin polarization; simulation box ~52 nm × 6 nm × 52 nm with 1,584,000 atomic sites; 270,000–500,000 MC cycles for convergence.. Test conditions: Energy pathway calculations at 0 K; dislocation motion simulations at 300 K under constant shear stress of 300 MPa; strain rate of 10^-3 s^-1 for CRSS estimation; activation barrier calculations via minimum energy path (MEP).. Findings: Configurational entropy (Sc) rarely reaches the ideal value (Sc,ideal); at 1650 K, Sc is ~95% of Sc,ideal, but drops significantly as LCO develops at lower Ta.; Complex stacking fault energy (CSFE) varies from -24.0 mJ/m² (random solid solution) to ~57 mJ/m² (strong LCO at 650 K).; Local antiphase boundary energies (APBEs) increase from ~50 mJ/m² to ~112 mJ/m² as Ta decreases from 1650 K to 650 K.; Twin boundary energy (γB) in LCO samples increases linearly with the number of transformed layers (λ), unlike elemental FCC metals where it converges.; Dislocations move via intermittent nanoscale segment detrapping (NSD) rather than smooth propagation, with effective barriers of ~0.15 eV even at 400 MPa shear stress.; Shear stress required to drive dislocation motion increases by a factor of three when the alloy is annealed at 650 K compared to the random state.; Critical resolved shear strength (CRSS) for the random NiCoCr state is ~70 MPa at 300 K and 10^-3 s^-1, consistent with experimental values of ~69 ± 3 MPa.. Mechanism: LCO creates a rugged energy landscape with spatially heterogeneous complex stacking fault energies (CSFE) and antiphase boundary energies (APBE). This heterogeneity acts as nanoscale obstacles that trap dislocation segments, forcing them to move via a nanoscale segment detrapping (NSD) mechanism. The energy required to break LCOs during slip and twinning increases activation barriers and lattice friction, leading to strengthening.. Limitations: The study uses a non-magnetic EAM potential which does not explicitly consider spin polarization; magnetic effects could alter energy differences by ~15 meV/atom. The simulations assume a single-phase solution without second-phase precipitation. Kinetic limitations in experiments may prevent the formation of predicted LCO states at low temperatures within typical homogenization times.. Future work: The authors propose using rapid cooling to obtain a random solid solution for ductility, followed by aging at elevated temperatures to induce LCO for strength. They suggest that the variability in LCO offers a new knob for property tuning in single-phase alloys.. Quote: "The LCO heightens the ruggedness of the energy landscape and raises activation barriers governing dislocation activities."

Paper card. Question: How does local chemical order (LCO) affect local dislocation segment activation barriers in multi-principal element alloys?. System: Multi-principal element alloys (specifically samples with equilibrium LCOs at Ta = 650, 950, and 1350 K). Processing: Hybrid MD and MC simulations on 20 nm × 20 nm × 10 nm samples (30 samples per condition) at Ta = 650, 950, and 1350 K; quenched to 0 K; cylinder configurations (20 nm diameter, 10 nm length) cut with a partial dislocation of screw character introduced; quasi-static athermal shearing employed; MEPs calculated using the simplified and improved string method with FIRE algorithm (reparameterization every 10 increments, convergence <10–3 Å or 3000 iterations). Test conditions: Temperatures of 650 K, 950 K, and 1350 K for equilibrium LCO; 0 K for energy minimization; athermal stress limit via quasi-static shearing. Findings: 30 different samples were obtained for each processing condition to ensure meaningful statistics; Sample dimensions were 20 nm × 20 nm × 10 nm along x[11¯0], y[1¯1¯1¯], and z[112¯]; Cylinder configurations had a diameter of 20 nm and axial direction along [112¯]; Dislocation line length was 10 nm as detrapping processes are on the nanoscale; Outer layers of atoms with thickness >2x potential cutoff radius were fixed during energy minimization; Inner cylindrical region with 10 nm diameter was used to calculate average local shear stress; Convergence criterion for MEP calculation was displacement <10–3 Å or 3000 iterations. Mechanism: The authors employed hybrid MD and MC simulations to obtain equilibrium LCOs and then used the string method to calculate minimum energy pathways (MEPs) for dislocation segments, aiming to examine LCO effects on local dislocation segment activation barriers.. Quote: "In order to examine the LCO effects on local dislocation segment activation barriers, hybrid MD and MC simulations were performed"

card: Paper card. Question: How can the strength–ductility trade-off inherent to traditional alloys be overcome in multi-principal-element alloys by exploiting multiple levels of heterogeneities?. System: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) and medium-entropy alloys (MEAs) including FCC-based systems (e.g., CoCrFeNi, CrCoNi, VCoNi), BCC-based refractory systems (e.g., TiZrHfNbTa), dual-phase eutectic lamella HEAs, and alloys with multicomponent intermetallic nanoparticles (MCINPs). Processing: Partial recrystallization to create heterogeneous grain structures (HGS), spinodal decomposition to form precipitates, addition of oxygen solutes (~2 at%) to form nanoscale complexes, and intentional alloying to tune stacking fault energy (SFE) for deformation-induced transformations. Test conditions: Room temperature (RT) uniaxial tensile testing; cryogenic temperatures (77 K and 4 K) for specific FCC MEAs; compression testing for some refractory BCC HEAs. Findings: An FCC-MCINP alloy achieved a yield strength above 1 GPa with a uniform elongation (εu) of ~50%, showing no strength–ductility trade-off compared to unstrengthened elemental metals.; A single-phase CrCoNi MEA with a heterogeneous grain structure (HGS) spanning nano-to-micro scales reached a gigapascal yield strength while maintaining εu in excess of 20%.; The VCoNi MEA achieved near-GPa yield strength with εu ~30% and total elongation ~38%, attributed to maximized lattice friction from atomic size mismatch.; In BCC-TiZrHfNb HEA, adding ~2 at% oxygen formed nanoscale (O, Ti, Zr)-complexes that increased tensile elongation from ~14% to ~28% while maintaining high strength.; Stress-assisted martensitic transformation in BCC-Ti35Zr27.5Hf27.5Nb5Ta5 HEA created a 65% volume fraction of internally twinned martensite, doubling the strain-hardening rate.; Wide hysteresis loops in load–unload–reload stress–strain curves demonstrated that nonhomogeneous plastic deformation in HGS alloys imparts high back stresses contributing to strain hardening.; At cryogenic temperatures (77 K and 4 K), the CrCoNi MEA exhibited strain-hardening rates and εu comparable to the best 316 austenitic stainless steels due to reduced dynamic recovery.. Mechanism: The authors argue that the high concentration of multiple principal elements creates a rugged energy landscape with statistical fluctuations in composition and local chemical order (LCO), causing dislocations to adopt a wavy line and face intermittent 'nanoscale segment detrapping' barriers. This intrinsic lattice friction is compounded by a hierarchy of heterogeneities (defects, precipitates, grain boundaries, phase boundaries) that promote nonhomogeneous plastic deformation, geometrically necessary dislocation storage, and dynamic mechanisms like twinning (TWIP) and transformation (TRIP), which sustain high strain-hardening rates to delay necking.. Limitations: Refractory BCC HEAs often lack room-temperature tensile ductility due to a drastic rise in the ductile-to-brittle transition temperature; TRIP-assisted DP alloys with low initial yield strength require hardening (e.g., cold work) which causes the strain-hardening rate to become inadequate, restoring the strength–ductility trade-off at high σy levels.. Future work: Continued endeavors to tailor heterogeneities to ward off plastic instabilities and realize even better strength–ductility balance, expanding the repertoire of alloys in compositions and properties through refined and enhanced HEAs.. Quote: "The strength of HEAs is considerably higher than traditional solid solutions, as the many constituents lead to a rugged energy landscape that increases the resistance to dislocation motion."

card: Paper card. Question: How does chemical complexity in single-phase concentrated solid solution alloys (SP-CSAs) affect the migration range and evolution of radiation-induced defects compared to pure nickel under ion irradiation?. System: Single crystalline pure nickel (Ni), 50%Ni50%Co (NiCo), and 50%Ni50%Fe (NiFe) with fcc structure. Processing: Ion beam irradiation using 3 MeV Au ions at room temperature to fluences of 2 × 10^13/cm^2, ~1 × 10^14/cm^2, and ~5 × 10^15/cm^2; samples prepared via FIB lift-out followed by flash polishing (4% perchloric acid in 96% ethanol, 6~14 V, -30 to -50 °C, 0.05-0.2 s). Test conditions: Room temperature irradiation; cross-sectional TEM (300 keV, g=[200]), RBS-C (3.5 MeV He+ ions), k-ART simulations (300 K and 900 K), and MD simulations (40 keV PKA). Findings: Defect clusters in pure Ni stretched to 550 nm at 2 × 10^13/cm^2 and ~1,100 nm at 5 × 10^15/cm^2, exceeding SRIM predictions.; Defect clusters in NiCo and NiFe reached ~460 nm and ~460 nm respectively at low fluence, and ~900 nm and ~800 nm at high fluence.; The damage range in pure Ni was significantly deeper than in NiCo and NiFe at high fluence, indicating higher defect migration rates in pure Ni.; Vacancy-type stacking fault tetrahedra (SFT) and interstitial loops coexist in the same region, consistent with MD simulations.; k-ART simulations showed small vacancy clusters (di-vacancies, tri-vacancies) have migration barriers of 0.3–0.4 eV, making them highly mobile at room temperature.; RBS-C measurements showed damage ranges slightly shallower than TEM (e.g., NiCo: 350 nm vs 460 nm at low fluence) due to density assumptions.; High-fluence irradiation (1.1 × 10^17/cm^2) induced high-level mechanical stress, with implanted Au atoms occupying lattice sites (~7% concentration).. Mechanism: The extended damage range beyond the theoretical ion stopping depth is attributed to the migration of highly mobile small vacancy clusters and interstitials, prolonged irradiation time allowing further diffusion, and mechanical stress gradients from implanted Au ions driving defects deeper. The slower migration in alloys is caused by higher defect migration barriers due to intrinsic chemical disorder and lattice distortion, which localize energy dissipation and enhance defect recombination.. Limitations: The text notes that RBS-C depth calculations assume un-irradiated sample density, ignoring potential irradiation-induced volume swelling, and that the 'knee' point method for determining damage range relies on assumptions that may not align perfectly with TEM criteria.. Future work: The authors propose that the chemical species of SP-CSA alloys on defect migration should be studied in further detail, particularly by computer simulation.. Quote: "Defects in nickel migrate faster than in NiCo and NiFe."

card: Paper card. Question: How can short-range order (SRO) be detected in medium/high-entropy alloys (MEAs/HEAs) using non-imaging and imaging techniques, and what is the impact of SRO on their physical and mechanical properties?. System: NiCoCr medium-entropy alloy (MEA), CrMnFeCoNi and CrFeCoNiPd high-entropy alloys (HEAs), VNiCo MEA, Ru-based HEA nanoparticles (NPs), and a 15-element HEA (15-HEA). Processing: Synthesis of NiCoCr samples followed by two heat treatments: water-quenching after homogenization at 1,200°C, and aging at 1,000°C for 120 h followed by slow furnace cooling; synthesis of VNiCo MEA; synthesis of Ru-based HEA NPs via carbothermal shock; irradiation of NiCoCr with Ni ions at doses up to 0.3 displacements per atoms (dpa). Test conditions: X-ray diffraction (XRD), neutron diffraction, X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS/EXAFS), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), high-angle annular dark-field scanning TEM (HAADF-STEM), energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS), geometric phase analysis (GPA), nano-indentation, bulk tensile tests, and irradiation tests. Findings: In NiCoCr MEA, EXAFS fitting revealed that Cr atoms favored bonding with Ni and Co atoms, while Cr-Cr bonds were disfavored, indicated by a larger Debye-Waller (DW) factor for Cr-Cr bonds compared to Cr-Ni and Cr-Co bonds.; Aging NiCoCr MEA at 1,000°C for 120 h followed by slow cooling resulted in superlattice streaking in diffraction patterns and contrast in dark-field images, indicating increased SRO compared to water-quenched samples.; In VNiCo MEA, EDS mapping showed an alternating pattern of V-enriched regions sandwiching Co- or Ni-enriched regions, with a spacing of less than 1 nm, confirming SRO.; Irradiation of NiCoCr MEA to 0.3 dpa decreased Ni-Cr bond distances from 2.51 Å to 2.49 Å and reduced DW factors from 0.002 Å² to 0.001 Å², suggesting radiation increases the amount of SRO.; The aged NiCoCr MEA showed a 25% increase in yield point compared to the water-quenched sample, confirming the strengthening effect of SRO.; The stacking fault energy (SFE) for the aged NiCoCr sample was double that of the water-quenched sample, indicating a positive correlation between SRO degree and SFE.; In VNiCo MEA, SRO-dislocation coupling was observed, where dislocations were sluggish through SRO domains, leading to increased strain hardening during tensile deformation.; APT analysis of annealed NiCoCr MEA showed peak intensity variations spanning approximately 2 nm, classified as local chemical ordering (LCO) rather than typical SRO.. Mechanism: SRO arises from preferential bonding between specific elements (e.g., Cr-Ni/Co in NiCoCr, V-Co/Ni in VNiCo), leading to local lattice distortions and alternating chemical planes. These distortions create energetically favorable domains that impede dislocation motion (SRO-dislocation coupling), increasing yield strength and strain hardening. Radiation exposure can enhance SRO by altering bond distances and reducing lattice disorder.. Limitations: XRD and neutron diffraction total scattering measurements were not able to identify evidence of ordering in NiCoCr MEA because PDF analysis could not distinguish bond lengths and vibrations of pairs of atoms with comparable atomic sizes. TEM imaging alone could not determine the exact bonding preferences causing alternating contrast; element-specific methods were required. Most studies focused on MEAs with 3d transition metals, limiting understanding of more complex HEAs with 4d or 5d metals.. Future work: Conduct studies on HEA samples containing higher numbers of elements and combinations of 3d, 4d, and 5d transition metals to uncover how SRO arises in a wider compositional space. Prepare samples with varying degrees of SRO through controlled heat treatments to accurately assess the impact of SRO on mechanical properties. Investigate the impact of SRO on the catalytic properties of HEA nanoparticles. Develop new non-imaging and imaging techniques, such as 4D-STEM and atom probe tomography (APT), to better characterize SRO.. Quote: "Cr atoms favored bonding with Ni and Co atoms, and disfavored forming bonds with other Cr atoms."

card: Paper card. Question: What are the atomistic to micro-scale mechanisms underlying the exceptional damage tolerance (high strength, ductility, and fracture toughness) of the single-phase CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy?. System: CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (single-phase fcc solid solution). Processing: Arc-melting high-purity elemental starting materials, drop casting into copper moulds, cold forging and cross rolling at room temperature, recrystallization at 800 °C (grain size ∼6 μm), followed by ion milling (5 kV) or twin jet polishing (10 °C, 13 mA/12 V) to create electron-transparent foils with cracks. Test conditions: In situ straining in an aberration-corrected TEM (FEI Tecnai G2 F20, 200 kV) at room temperature using pulsed tensile loading (axial displacement rate ∼1.0 μm s⁻¹). Findings: Early deformation is dominated by the easy motion of Shockley partial dislocations (1/6<112> type) and the continuous nucleation/annihilation of stacking faults (SFs).; Interactions between partials on different {111} planes form stable 'stacking-fault parallelepipeds' (volume defects) that act as formidable obstacles for dislocation motion.; Perfect (undissociated, 1/2<110> type) dislocations move with extreme difficulty in localized bands of planar slip, creating strong barriers that arrest fast-moving partial dislocations.; The motion of perfect dislocations requires overcoming continuous activation barriers, indicative of high friction stress in the alloy.; Nanoscale voids form in the 'semi-cohesive zone' at the intersection of two {111} slip planes, creating fiber-like bridges spanning the crack faces.; These nanobridges (size <200 nm, some ∼100 nm) deform primarily via nano-twinning ({111} twin structure), which accommodates strain and shields the crack tip.; The synergy of these mechanisms yields tensile strength ∼1 GPa, ductility ∼60–70%, and fracture toughness K_JIc > 200 MPa√m.. Mechanism: The authors propose a synergistic sequence where intrinsic toughening arises from easy partial dislocation motion (ductility) followed by strain hardening via stacking-fault parallelepipeds and planar slip bands (strength). Extrinsic toughening occurs via nanoscale twinned bridges that form behind the crack tip, carrying load and shielding the crack tip from the applied driving force.. Limitations: The study notes that 'ultrahigh-resolution observations have to be made at the nanoscale to permit any characterization of mechanisms so close to the crack tip,' and that 'thin foil samples must be used which, under load, cannot display the full constraint of a bulk sample.'. Future work: The authors state that 'further optimization of these mechanisms may present new directions for the future design of advanced metallic materials with unprecedented damage tolerance.'. Quote: "We identify a synergy of multiple deformation mechanisms, rarely achieved in metallic alloys, which generates high strength, work hardening and ductility"

card: Paper card. Question: How can the miscibility gap in bimetallic Co-Mo alloys be overcome to create tunable, highly active catalysts for ammonia decomposition using earth-abundant elements?. System: Quinary CoMoFeNiCu high-entropy alloy nanoparticles (general composition CoxMoyFe10Ni10Cu10 where x + y = 70) and control samples of bimetallic Co-Mo and monometallic Ru. Processing: Carbothermal shock technique involving flash heating and cooling of metal precursors on oxygenated carbon nanofibers; temperature reached 2000–2300 K with ramping rates on the order of 10^5 K s−1 and shock duration of ~55 ms. Test conditions: Ammonia decomposition in a plug flow reactor at 250–600 °C using 5 vol% NH3 (and 100 vol% NH3 for specific tests) at a gas hourly space velocity (GHSV) of 36 L gcat−1 h−1. Findings: HEA-Co25Mo45 achieved a mass-specific reaction rate of 22.1 gNH3 gmetals−1 h−1 at 500 °C, representing an improvement factor of ~19 versus bimetallic Co-Mo and ~3 versus Ru.; The most active catalyst, HEA-Co25Mo45, reached 50% NH3 conversion (T50) at 422 °C, compared to 600 °C for Ru and 600 °C for bimetallic Co-Mo.; The apparent activation energy (Eapp) varied from 64.7 kJ mol−1 for the most active HEA-Co25Mo45 to 123.1 kJ mol−1 for the least active HEA-Co55Mo15.; Nitrogen desorption energy (ΔEN) for HEA-Co25Mo45 was ~79 kJ mol−1, which is very close to the value for Ru (84 kJ mol−1).; Catalytic activity exhibited a volcano-type behavior with respect to nitrogen adsorption energy, peaking at an optimal ΔEN of ~79 kJ mol−1.; The HEA-Co25Mo45 catalyst showed negligible degradation after ~50 hours of continuous operation at 500 °C.; For pure NH3 decomposition, HEA-Co55Mo15 achieved an improvement factor of ~118 versus bimetallic Co-Mo and ~40 versus Ru.; Atomistic modeling confirmed a single solid-solution phase with δ = 5.4% and ΔHmix = 0.65 kJ mol−1, showing no phase segregation up to 1000 K.. Mechanism: The high catalytic activity is attributed to the robust tuning of surface nitrogen binding strength via the Co/Mo ratio; the optimal activity arises from a tradeoff where Co-rich catalysts bind N too weakly (limiting dehydrogenation) and Mo-rich catalysts bind N too strongly (limiting N2 desorption), with the HEA composition allowing access to the optimal intermediate binding energy (~79 kJ mol−1) predicted by the Sabatier principle.. Limitations: The text notes that the peak intensities in XRD patterns are low due to the much smaller particle sizes compared to previously reported HEAs, and that the bimetallic Co-Mo catalysts are constrained by large miscibility gaps in their phase diagram.. Future work: The authors propose designing practical reactors with cascaded catalyst layers having gradually changing nitrogen binding strengths to match the varying concentration of NH3 along the flow, which can be readily achieved by varying the Co/Mo ratios in HEA catalysts.. Quote: "Quinary CoMoFeNiCu nanoparticles are synthesized in a single solid-solution phase with robust control over the Co/Mo atomic ratio, including those ratios considered to be immiscible according to the Co-Mo bimetallic phase diagram."

card: Paper card. Question: Does non-random chemical mixing (short-range ordering) exist in CrCoNi medium-entropy alloys, and how does it vary with thermomechanical history and influence dislocation slip behavior?. System: CrCoNi medium-entropy alloy (equiatomic Cr, Co, Ni). Processing: Arc melting and drop casting (5x repetition) followed by homogenization at 1200 °C for 48 h; one sample water-quenched (WQ), the other aged at 1000 °C for 120 h followed by furnace cooling (HT). Test conditions: Room temperature tensile testing at a strain rate of 1 × 10−3 s−1; electron nanodiffraction (SEND) with 1.1 mrad semi-convergence angle and 10 eV energy filter; Small-Angle Neutron Scattering (SANS); Atom Probe Tomography (APT) at 50 K base temperature. Findings: Two types of short-range order (SRO) were identified: L12 (minimizing Cr–Cr nearest neighbors) and L11 (segregating Cr on alternating close-packed planes).; In the water-quenched (WQ) sample, L11-type nanoclusters are predominant, whereas in the heat-treated (HT) sample, L12-type nanoclusters become more dominant.; The L12-type diffuse peaks are split, a feature consistent with Fermi surface nesting mechanisms observed in binary alloys like CuPd.; Estimated SRO parameters for L12 ordering are α_CrCo = α_CrNi = −0.18, consistent with Monte-Carlo DFT theory predictions.; Dislocation slip behavior changes drastically: WQ shows wavy dislocations mixed with localized planar slips, while HT exhibits extensive planar slips with paired dislocations.; SANS detected scattering objects with a Guinier radius of gyration Rg ~ 3.0 Å in both samples, indicating sub-nm chemical fluctuations.; APT analysis revealed Ni-rich and Cr-poor nanoclusters of a few nm in size with negative Ni-Cr and Co-Cr correlations.; Yield strengths were similar for both samples (227 MPa for WQ and 224 MPa for HT), attributed to the presence of CSRO in both.. Mechanism: The L12-type ordering is driven by magnetic interactions (minimizing Cr–Cr pairs in favor of Cr–Co/Cr–Ni) and Fermi surface instability, while L11-type ordering involves segregation on alternating {111} planes. The destruction of L12-type CSRO by leading dislocations creates diffuse antiphase boundaries with higher energy, causing paired dislocations to form to reduce energy costs, resulting in a glide plane softening effect and extensive planar slip.. Limitations: The study notes that neither the L11 nor L12 CSRO models explain the (3̄11)/2 diffuse spot observed in cold-rolled samples by previous researchers, indicating multiplicity of local bonding preferences dependent on history. Additionally, standard atomic-resolution STEM imaging showed no obvious evidence of CSRO, highlighting the need for the developed data-driven approach.. Future work: The authors suggest the methodology provides general opportunities for atomistic-structure study in concentrated alloys for the design of strong and ductile materials, and imply further investigation into the specific role of magnetic interactions and Fermi surface instabilities in driving CSRO.. Quote: "Two samples, one homogenized and one heat-treated, are observed. In both samples, results reveal two types of short-range-order inside nanoclusters that minimize the Cr–Cr nearest neighbors (L12) or segregate Cr on alternating close-packed planes (L11)."

card: Paper card. Question: How does the crystal-glass duality (presence vs. absence of a crystal lattice) affect the electronic transport properties of the Al0.5TiZrPdCuNi alloy when prepared as a high-entropy alloy (HEA) versus a metallic glass (MG) at the same chemical composition?. System: Al0.5TiZrPdCuNi (6-component alloy; nominal composition Al7.0Ti21.1Zr15.3Pd14.0Cu21.3Ni21.3 at.% in MG; bcc + Pd2TiAl-type cubic phases in HEA). Processing: MG: Melt spinning to produce ribbons of 20 µm thickness and 1 mm width; HEA: Conventional Cu-mold casting to produce rods of 1.3 mm² cross-section (or melt spinning at slower cooling rates); both prepared at the same nominal chemical composition.. Test conditions: Electrical resistivity, thermopower, thermal conductivity, Hall coefficient, specific heat, and magnetic susceptibility measured between 2 K and 400 K; Hall coefficient measured in magnetic fields μ0H = ±9 T; specific heat measured between 1.8 K and 4.5 K.. Findings: Both HEA and MG states exhibit negative-temperature-coefficient (NTC) resistivity, with ρ400K_MG = 277 µΩ cm and ρ400K_HEA = 157 µΩ cm.; The NTC magnitude is 7% for the MG sample (ρ2K = 295 µΩ cm) compared to 3% for the HEA sample (ρ2K = 162 µΩ cm).; Thermopower is positive for both, with S380K_HEA = 7.3 µV K⁻¹, which is a factor of ~2 larger than S380K_MG = 3.2 µV K⁻¹.; Thermal conductivity values converge at high temperature: κ390K_MG = κ390K_HEA = 8.2 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹.; Hall coefficients are positive and nearly identical: RH_MG = 3.7 × 10⁻¹¹ m³ C⁻¹ and RH_HEA = 3.2 × 10⁻¹¹ m³ C⁻¹.; Electronic specific heat coefficients are γ_HEA = 2.91 mJ mol⁻¹ K⁻² and γ_MG = 2.28 mJ mol⁻¹ K⁻², yielding a DOS ratio g_HEA/g_MG = 1.27.; Both samples exhibit Pauli spin paramagnetism with total magnetic susceptibility χ ≈ 1 × 10⁻⁹ m³ mol⁻¹.; The ratio of spectral conductivities at the Fermi level is σ_HEA/σ_MG = 1.8, while the ratio of electronic mobilities is μ_e_HEA/μ_e_MG ≈ 1.4–1.5.. Mechanism: The immense chemical (substitutional) disorder and associated topological disorder act as quenched defects that cause elastic scattering of conduction electrons at an extremely rapid rate (relaxation time τ₀ ~ 10⁻¹⁵ s), making phonon contribution to transport negligible. The temperature dependence of transport coefficients originates predominantly from the temperature dependence of the Fermi-Dirac function and the variation of the spectral conductivity (and electronic density of states) with energy within the Fermi-level region. The positive Hall coefficient is explained by the negative derivative of the electronic density of states at the Fermi energy (RH ∝ -dg/dε|εF).. Limitations: The HEA state is a quenched metastable state rather than the equilibrium multi-phase crystalline state; the theoretical analysis assumes spatial isotropy and neglects the Landau orbital diamagnetic contribution; the Hall coefficient mechanism in disordered materials is noted as 'less understood' in the literature.. Quote: "The HEA and the MG states of the Al0.5TiZrPdCuNi alloy both show large, negative-temperature-coefficient resistivity, positive thermopower, positive Hall coefficient and small thermal conductivity."
